# Why Ecne is spelled that way — and what it costs to get it right

There is a version of this name the early internet had to settle for: *ecne*. This is the file on how **Ecne** replaced it.

Écne has the thinnest dossier of any figure in this collection — no surviving tale acts him, no epithet colors him, no treasure is laid in his hand. The tradition gives a name, a word, and a seat among the poets of the Túatha Dé Danann, and then it does something stranger and more honest: it tells the myths of the thing the name means. The mythology of Écne is the mythology of knowledge itself — the well, the hazels, the salmon, and everyone who ever burned a thumb on it.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Ecne
- **ASCII form:** ecne
- **Meaning:** "Knowledge"
- **Domain of influence:** Knowledge, Wisdom
- **Pantheon:** Celtic
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** —
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 105 of 397

## The Name Before the Marks


Spoken, the name runs `/ˈeː.ɡnʲe/` — 'EHG-nyeh' — hold a long tense 'eh' like French été, let the c melt into a soft g before the n, and finish with a light y-glide on the n and a short final vowel.

## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Ecne** lives at [/sites/ecne/](/sites/ecne/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/sites/ecne/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/sites/ecne/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/sites/ecne/patterns/).

Tier-2 here means one preserved truth — not less important, just singular. The temple shows it and names it.

## Where the Name Stood First

Écne is an entirely textual figure: no ogham stone names him, no votive inscription invokes him, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. The witnesses are manuscripts. Sanas Cormaic, the glossary that folds the word into the hazel-and-nut doctrine, is preserved in the great late-medieval Irish codices, among them the Yellow Book of Lecan and the Book of Ballymote; the Boyhood Deeds of Finn survives in late-medieval Irish manuscript tradition and was first put into modern print by Kuno Meyer in the opening volume of Ériu (1904). The material afterlife of the tradition is civic rather than ancient: John Kindness's Salmon of Knowledge — the ten-metre, tile-clad Big Fish raised on Donegall Quay, Belfast, in 1999 — is the largest monument the wisdom complex has ever received, its scales printed with the texts and images of the city's memory. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

## The Archetype at Work

The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) seats this temple in **3 industries**, each match argued and weighted: **Education, Research & Knowledge** (the name IS knowledge — the abstract made divine; the well of wisdom personified.); **Agriculture, Food & Harvest** (the nine hazels of wisdom dropping their nuts into the well — knowledge as harvest.); **History, Archives & Records** (fintan mac Bóchra remembers everything since the flood — knowledge held as living memory.). The [Resonance File](/sites/ecne/blog/resonance/) reads those seats through the myths themselves.
